steps.title: Convert to kelvin
steps.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to each Celsius temperature to get three hundred kelvin and three hundred and eight kelvin.

steps.title: Apply Charles's law
steps.narration: At constant pressure, volume is proportional to kelvin temperature, so multiply six hundred by three hundred and eight over three hundred.

steps.title: Calculate the volume
steps.narration: Six hundred divided by three hundred is two, and two times three hundred and eight gives six hundred and sixteen cubic centimetres. Choose D.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the initial volume and the two temperatures. Because pressure stays constant, Charles's law links the volume and temperature.

teach.title: Convert to kelvin
teach.narration: Change both temperatures from degrees Celsius to kelvin by adding two hundred and seventy-three, because gas law ratios only work on the absolute kelvin scale.

teach.title: State Charles's law
teach.narration: At constant pressure, volume divided by kelvin temperature stays constant. Rearrange the relation to solve for the new volume.

teach.title: Substitute the values
teach.narration: Substitute six hundred cubic centimetres, three hundred and eight kelvin, and three hundred kelvin. Six hundred over three hundred simplifies to two.

teach.title: Find the new volume
teach.narration: Multiply two by three hundred and eight to get six hundred and sixteen cubic centimetres. The air expands slightly as it warms up. Choose D.

steps.title: Convert to kelvin
steps.narration: Add two hundred and seventy-three to twenty-seven degrees Celsius to get three hundred kelvin.

steps.title: Use the ideal gas law
steps.narration: Rearrange P V equals n R T for pressure and substitute one mole, eight point three, three hundred kelvin, and ten to the minus two cubic metres.

steps.title: Simplify to standard form
steps.narration: Eight point three times three hundred gives two thousand four hundred and ninety, and dividing by ten to the minus two multiplies by one hundred. Choose C.

teach.title: List the given values
teach.narration: Write down one mole, the volume in cubic metres, and the temperature. The molar gas constant R is eight point three joules per mole kelvin.

teach.title: Convert temperature to kelvin
teach.narration: Change twenty-seven degrees Celsius to kelvin by adding two hundred and seventy-three, because the gas constant R uses kelvin.

teach.title: Rearrange the ideal gas law
teach.narration: Use the ideal gas equation because pressure, volume, moles, and temperature appear together. Divide both sides by volume to isolate pressure.

teach.title: Substitute and multiply
teach.narration: Multiply one by eight point three by three hundred on top to get two thousand four hundred and ninety.

teach.title: Write in standard form
teach.narration: Dividing by ten to the minus two is the same as multiplying by one hundred. Shifting the decimal point gives two point four nine times ten to the five newtons per square metre, option C.

steps.display: VP = 10 mm Hg, SVP = 17.50 mm Hg
steps.title: Identify the pressures
steps.narration: Read the actual vapour pressure of ten millimetres of mercury and the saturated vapour pressure of seventeen point five zero.

steps.title: Apply humidity formula
steps.narration: Divide actual vapour pressure by saturated vapour pressure and multiply by one hundred percent.

steps.title: Round the result
steps.narration: Ten divided by seventeen point five zero times one hundred is fifty-seven point one percent, which rounds to fifty-seven percent. Choose B.

teach.display: VP = 10 mm Hg, SVP = 17.50 mm Hg
teach.title: Pick out the pressures
teach.narration: Note both vapour pressures. The twenty degrees Celsius only confirms they are measured at the same temperature and is not needed in the calculation.

teach.title: State the humidity formula
teach.narration: Relative humidity compares the water vapour actually present in the air with the maximum it can hold at that temperature, expressed as a percentage.

teach.title: Substitute the pressures
teach.narration: Put ten on top and seventeen point five zero below, then multiply by one hundred so the fraction becomes a percentage.

teach.title: Divide and round
teach.narration: One thousand divided by seventeen point five gives about fifty-seven point one percent, which matches fifty-seven percent. Choose B.

steps.title: Convert time to seconds
steps.narration: Change two minutes into one hundred and twenty seconds so the time is in SI units.

steps.title: Find electrical heat
steps.narration: Multiply current, voltage, and time to get eighty-four thousand joules of heat energy.

steps.title: Find temperature rise
steps.narration: Divide eighty-four thousand joules by mass times specific heat capacity to get ten degrees Celsius. Choose C.

teach.display: m = 2 kg, I = 3.5 A, V = 200 V, t = 2 min
teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the mass of water, the current, the mains voltage, the heating time, and the specific heat capacity of four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram kelvin.

teach.title: Change minutes to seconds
teach.narration: Multiply two minutes by sixty to get one hundred and twenty seconds, because electrical energy in joules requires time in seconds.

teach.title: Calculate heat supplied
teach.narration: Multiply current, voltage, and time to find the electrical heat produced by the coil, which warms the water.

teach.title: Equate heat to temperature rise
teach.narration: Set the heat gained by the water equal to the electrical energy supplied, then divide by mass and specific heat capacity to isolate the temperature rise.

teach.title: Divide for the rise
teach.narration: Two times four thousand two hundred is eight thousand four hundred. Eighty-four thousand divided by eight thousand four hundred equals ten degrees Celsius. Choose C.

steps.title: Find the heat energy
steps.narration: Multiply one thousand watts by three hundred seconds to get three hundred thousand joules.

steps.title: Find temperature rise
steps.narration: Subtract thirty degrees Celsius from one hundred degrees Celsius to get a seventy degree rise.

steps.title: Solve for mass
steps.narration: Divide three hundred thousand by four thousand two hundred times seventy to get one point zero two kilograms. Choose C.

teach.title: Note the needed values
teach.narration: Record the power, heating time, and specific heat capacity. The two hundred and twenty volt rating is extra information we do not need because power in watts is already given.

teach.title: Find the temperature change
teach.narration: Subtract thirty degrees Celsius from one hundred degrees Celsius. A temperature rise of seventy Celsius degrees equals a rise of seventy kelvin.

teach.title: Compute energy supplied
teach.narration: Multiply power in watts by time in seconds to find the total electrical energy transferred as heat into the water.

teach.title: Rearrange for mass
teach.narration: Equate the heat gained by the water to the heater energy, then divide by specific heat capacity and temperature rise to isolate mass.

teach.title: Divide to find the mass
teach.narration: Four thousand two hundred times seventy is two hundred and ninety-four thousand. Dividing three hundred thousand by two hundred and ninety-four thousand gives about one point zero two kilograms, option C.

steps.title: Find total temperature drop
steps.narration: Subtract forty degrees Celsius from one hundred degrees Celsius across the whole bar.

steps.title: Scale to 60 cm
steps.narration: A well-lagged bar cools steadily along its length, so sixty centimetres gives a thirty-six degree drop.

steps.title: Subtract from hot end
steps.narration: Subtract thirty-six degrees Celsius from the hotter end at one hundred to get sixty-four degrees Celsius. Choose C.

teach.title: List the bar temperatures
teach.narration: The bar is one hundred centimetres long, kept at one hundred degrees Celsius at one end and forty degrees Celsius at the other.

teach.title: Find temperature gradient
teach.narration: Because the bar is well-lagged, no heat leaks out the sides and temperature drops uniformly at zero point six degrees Celsius per centimetre.

teach.title: Find the drop at 60 cm
teach.narration: Multiply the gradient by sixty centimetres because the question measures sixty centimetres from the hotter end.

teach.title: Subtract from the hotter end
teach.narration: Start from one hundred degrees Celsius at the hotter end and subtract the thirty-six degree drop as we move toward the cooler end.

teach.title: Read the temperature
teach.narration: The temperature sixty centimetres from the hot end is sixty-four degrees Celsius. Choose C.

steps.title: Read period from graph
steps.narration: From the diagram, one full crest and trough ends at zero point two seconds.

steps.title: Use frequency formula
steps.narration: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period, so divide one by zero point two seconds.

steps.title: Find the frequency
steps.narration: One divided by zero point two gives five hertz. Choose C.

teach.title: Read the wave graph
teach.narration: Read the horizontal time axis on the diagram. One full cycle, one crest plus one trough, runs from zero to zero point two seconds, giving period T equals zero point two seconds. The zero point zero one centimetre amplitude marked on the vertical axis is extra information not needed for frequency.

teach.title: Relate frequency and period
teach.narration: Frequency is the number of complete waves in one second, which is the reciprocal of the time for one wave.

teach.title: Substitute the period
teach.narration: Put zero point two seconds into the denominator. Multiplying top and bottom by ten turns one over zero point two into ten over two.

teach.title: Calculate the frequency
teach.narration: Ten divided by two equals five cycles per second, or five hertz. Choose C.

steps.title: Compare wave equation
steps.narration: Match the given equation against the standard progressive wave equation.

steps.title: Match the x coefficient
steps.narration: The number multiplying x is zero point four, so set two pi over wavelength equal to zero point four.

steps.title: Solve for wavelength
steps.narration: Divide two pi by zero point four to get fifteen point seven metres. Choose B.

teach.title: Inspect the wave equation
teach.narration: Look at the term multiplying x inside the bracket, which is zero point four. The amplitude five and the two thousand pi term in front of t are extra information not needed to find the wavelength.

teach.title: Recall standard wave form
teach.narration: In the standard progressive wave formula, the coefficient of x equals two pi divided by the wavelength because a shift of one wavelength changes the angle by two pi radians.

teach.title: Equate x coefficients
teach.narration: Match the x coefficients in both equations by setting two pi over wavelength equal to zero point four.

teach.title: Rearrange for wavelength
teach.narration: Swap wavelength and zero point four, then use pi equals three point one four two so two pi is six point two eight four.

teach.title: Divide for wavelength
teach.narration: Six point two eight four divided by zero point four is fifteen point seven one, which matches fifteen point seven metres. Choose B.

steps.title: Use the echo formula
steps.narration: Sound goes down to the seabed and back again, so divide speed times time by two.

steps.title: Substitute speed and time
steps.narration: Multiply one thousand five hundred metres per second by four seconds and divide by two.

steps.title: Find the sea depth
steps.narration: Six thousand divided by two gives three thousand metres. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the speed of sound in seawater and the four seconds taken for the echo to return.

teach.title: Account for the round trip
teach.narration: An echo travels down to the bottom of the sea and back up to the source, covering twice the sea depth. Divide the round-trip distance by two to find the depth.

teach.title: Substitute and multiply
teach.narration: Multiply one thousand five hundred metres per second by four seconds to get six thousand metres for the total path there and back.

teach.title: Halve for the depth
teach.narration: Half of six thousand metres is three thousand metres. Choose B.

steps.title: Convert length to metres
steps.narration: Divide forty-five centimetres by one hundred to get zero point four five metres.

steps.title: Find fundamental wavelength
steps.narration: For a closed pipe, the fundamental wavelength is four times the pipe length.

steps.title: Find the frequency
steps.narration: Divide three hundred and sixty metres per second by one point eight zero metres to get two hundred point zero hertz. Choose C.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the pipe length, the speed of sound in air, and that the pipe is closed at one end.

teach.title: Change centimetres to metres
teach.narration: Convert forty-five centimetres to metres because the sound velocity is in metres per second and formulas need matching SI units.

teach.title: Find closed-pipe wavelength
teach.narration: In the fundamental note of a closed pipe, one quarter of a wave fits between the closed node and open antinode, so one full wavelength is four times the pipe length.

teach.title: Apply wave speed formula
teach.narration: Frequency equals wave speed divided by wavelength. Substitute three hundred and sixty metres per second and one point eight zero metres.

teach.title: Calculate frequency
teach.narration: Three hundred and sixty divided by one point eight zero equals two hundred point zero hertz. Choose C.

steps.title: Use string proportionality
steps.narration: For a stretched string, frequency varies directly with the square root of tension and inversely with length.

steps.title: Find the scale factor
steps.narration: Four times tension gives a factor of root four, which is two, while doubling length divides by two.

steps.title: Find the new frequency
steps.narration: The two changes cancel out, so the frequency stays four hundred hertz. Choose B.

teach.title: List what changes
teach.narration: Start with the original frequency of four hundred hertz, then note that length doubles while tension becomes four times as large.

teach.title: State the string formula
teach.narration: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string depends on length, tension, and the mass per unit length of the string.

teach.title: Track changing quantities
teach.narration: Because it is the same string, its mass per unit length stays constant, so we only compare the square root of tension over length.

teach.title: Find the net factor
teach.narration: The square root of four multiplies frequency by two, while doubling length divides it by two, leaving an overall factor of one.

teach.title: Find the new frequency
teach.narration: Multiplying four hundred hertz by one leaves the note at four hundred hertz. Choose B.

steps.title: Relate frequency and force
steps.narration: For a fixed length of wire, frequency is proportional to the square root of the stretching force.

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.narration: The square roots of three hundred and twenty-four and two hundred and twenty-five are eighteen and fifteen, giving one point two.

steps.title: Find the new frequency
steps.narration: Multiply two hundred and fifty-five by one point two to get three hundred and six hertz. Choose C.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the original frequency and the two stretching forces applied to the same wire.

teach.title: Use tension proportionality
teach.narration: Because the wire length and linear density stay fixed, frequency grows with the square root of the stretching force.

teach.title: Substitute and take roots
teach.narration: Put three hundred and twenty-four over two hundred and twenty-five inside the root. Eighteen squared is three hundred and twenty-four and fifteen squared is two hundred and twenty-five.

teach.title: Simplify the ratio
teach.narration: Divide eighteen and fifteen by three to get six fifths, which equals one point two.

teach.title: Find the new frequency
teach.narration: Multiply two hundred and fifty-five hertz by one point two to get three hundred and six hertz. Choose C.

steps.title: Find the magnification
steps.narration: Divide the image distance of forty centimetres by the object distance of ten centimetres to get four.

steps.title: Multiply by object height
steps.narration: Multiply the magnification of four by the object height of three centimetres.

steps.title: Read the image height
steps.narration: Four times three gives twelve point zero zero centimetres. Choose D.

teach.display: h_{o} = 3 cm, u = 10 cm, v = 40 cm
teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the object height, how far the object is from the mirror, and how far the image forms.

teach.title: Find linear magnification
teach.narration: Magnification equals image distance divided by object distance. Dividing forty by ten shows the image is four times as tall as the object.

teach.title: Link magnification to height
teach.narration: Because magnification also equals image height over object height, multiply magnification by object height to find image height.

teach.title: Calculate image height
teach.narration: Multiply four by three centimetres to get twelve point zero zero centimetres. Choose D.

steps.title: Find the focal length
steps.narration: Halve the thirty-six centimetre radius of curvature to get an eighteen centimetre focal length.

steps.title: Apply the mirror formula
steps.narration: A real image three times as large means v equals three u, so combine the left side to four over three u.

steps.title: Solve for object distance
steps.narration: Cross-multiply to get three u equals seventy-two, then divide by three to get twenty-four centimetres. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the mirror's radius of curvature is thirty-six centimetres and the real image is three times the object's size.

teach.title: Find the focal length
teach.narration: The focal length of a concave mirror is half its radius of curvature, which gives eighteen centimetres, positive for a converging mirror.

teach.title: Express v using u
teach.narration: Because the image is real, image distance is positive and equals three times the object distance.

teach.title: Substitute in mirror formula
teach.narration: Put v equals three u into the mirror equation and add the fractions using common denominator three u.

teach.title: Solve for object distance
teach.narration: Cross-multiply to get three u equals seventy-two, then divide by three to get twenty-four centimetres. Choose B.

steps.title: Use the lens formula
steps.narration: Subtract one over sixty from one over twenty to find one over the image distance.

steps.title: Find image distance
steps.narration: Inverting gives thirty point zero centimetres, so the magnification is zero point five.

steps.title: Find the image size
steps.narration: Multiply zero point five by the three point zero centimetre object height to get one point five centimetres. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the object height, object distance, and focal length of the converging lens.

teach.title: Rearrange the lens formula
teach.narration: Start from one over u plus one over v equals one over f, and move one over u to the right to solve for image distance.

teach.title: Find image distance
teach.narration: Use common denominator sixty to subtract, giving one over thirty, so the real image forms thirty point zero centimetres from the lens.

teach.title: Calculate magnification
teach.narration: Divide image distance by object distance. Because sixty is beyond twice the focal length, the image is smaller, with magnification zero point five.

teach.title: Find the image height
teach.narration: Multiply magnification zero point five by three point zero centimetres to get an image size of one point five centimetres. Choose B.

steps.title: Find light speed in glass
steps.narration: Divide the speed of light in vacuum by the refractive index one point five zero.

steps.title: Convert thickness to metres
steps.narration: Change zero point nine centimetres into nine times ten to the minus three metres.

steps.title: Calculate transit time
steps.narration: Divide the thickness in metres by the speed in glass to get four point five times ten to the minus eleven seconds. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the plate thickness, the refractive index of the glass, and the speed of light in a vacuum.

teach.title: Find speed in glass
teach.narration: Light slows down inside glass by a factor equal to the refractive index, so divide three point zero times ten to the eight by one point five zero.

teach.title: Change centimetres to metres
teach.narration: Convert zero point nine centimetres to metres so the thickness matches the metres per second unit of speed.

teach.title: Divide distance by speed
teach.narration: Time equals distance divided by speed. Put the plate thickness over the speed of light inside glass.

teach.title: Simplify powers of ten
teach.narration: Nine divided by two gives four point five, and minus three minus eight gives exponent minus eleven seconds. Choose B.

steps.title: Find series capacitance
steps.narration: Add the reciprocals of two, six, and three microfarads to get equivalent capacitance one microfarad.

steps.title: Find the shared charge
steps.narration: Series capacitors share the same charge, so multiply one microfarad by twelve volts to get twelve microcoulombs.

steps.title: Find each voltage
steps.narration: Divide twelve microcoulombs by two, six, and three microfarads to get six, two, and four volts. Choose D.

teach.title: Read the circuit diagram
teach.narration: From the diagram, a twelve volt battery drives a single series branch containing C one equal to two microfarads, C two equal to six microfarads, and C three equal to three microfarads.

teach.title: Find series capacitance
teach.narration: For capacitors in series, reciprocals add. Using common denominator six gives six over six, so the combined capacitance is one microfarad.

teach.title: Find the common charge
teach.narration: Multiply equivalent capacitance by supply voltage. Because the capacitors are in one series line, each holds twelve microcoulombs of charge.

teach.title: Find voltage across C1
teach.narration: Potential difference equals charge divided by capacitance, so dividing twelve microcoulombs by two microfarads gives six volts across C one.

teach.title: Find V2 and V3
teach.narration: Divide twelve by six to get two volts across C two, and twelve by three to get four volts across C three. Notice six plus two plus four equals twelve volts. Choose D.

steps.title: List both capacitances
steps.narration: Note the capacitance in air is three microfarads and with the dielectric is six microfarads.

steps.title: Take the ratio
steps.narration: Dielectric constant equals capacitance with the dielectric divided by capacitance in air.

steps.title: Find the dielectric constant
steps.narration: Six divided by three equals two. Choose C.

teach.title: List the capacitances
teach.narration: Write down the capacitor's value in air and its larger value when the dielectric material fills the space between the plates.

teach.title: Define dielectric constant
teach.narration: Inserting a dielectric multiplies capacitance by the dielectric constant, so divide the dielectric capacitance by the air capacitance.

teach.title: Substitute the values
teach.narration: Put six microfarads over three microfarads. Both are in microfarads, so the units cancel directly.

teach.title: Divide for the answer
teach.narration: Six divided by three gives a dielectric constant of two. Choose C.

steps.title: State the force formula
steps.narration: Electric force on a charge equals the charge multiplied by the electric field intensity.

steps.title: Substitute charge and field
steps.narration: Multiply one point five times ten to the minus nineteen coulombs by ten to the five volts per metre.

steps.title: Combine powers of ten
steps.narration: Adding minus nineteen and five gives minus fourteen, so the force is one point five times ten to the minus fourteen newtons. Choose C.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the charge given in coulombs and the electric field intensity in volts per metre, both already in SI units.

teach.title: State electric force law
teach.narration: Electric field intensity means force per unit charge, so multiplying the charge by the field gives the force on the electron.

teach.title: Substitute the values
teach.narration: Put the given charge and field strength into the formula.

teach.title: Add the exponents
teach.narration: Add the exponents of ten: minus nineteen plus five equals minus fourteen. The force is one point five times ten to the minus fourteen newtons, option C.

steps.title: Convert to farads
steps.narration: Change eight microfarads to eight times ten to the minus six farads.

steps.title: Use the energy formula
steps.narration: Substitute capacitance in farads and one hundred volts into half C V squared.

steps.title: Find stored energy
steps.narration: Four times ten to the minus six times ten to the four equals four point zero times ten to the minus two joules. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the capacitance in microfarads and the potential difference across the capacitor.

teach.title: Convert microfarads to farads
teach.narration: Multiply by ten to the minus six to convert microfarads into farads because stored energy in joules requires SI units.

teach.title: State the energy formula
teach.narration: The energy stored in a capacitor equals half times capacitance times potential difference squared.

teach.title: Substitute C and V
teach.narration: Put eight times ten to the minus six farads and one hundred volts into the equation. Half of eight is four, and one hundred squared is ten to the four.

teach.title: Simplify powers of ten
teach.narration: Add the exponents minus six and four to get minus two. The energy stored is four point zero times ten to the minus two joules, option B.

steps.title: Write the balance ratio
steps.narration: In a metre bridge, the left and right resistances match the ratio of the left and right wire lengths.

steps.title: Cross-multiply and collect
steps.narration: Cross-multiplying gives two hundred minus two l equals three l, so five l equals two hundred.

steps.title: Find the balance point
steps.narration: Divide two hundred by five to get forty centimetres from the left side. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the two ohm and three ohm resistors in the left and right gaps, and recall that a metre bridge wire is one hundred centimetres long.

teach.title: State balance condition
teach.narration: At balance, no current flows through the galvanometer, so the ratio of left to right resistance equals the ratio of left to right wire lengths.

teach.title: Substitute the resistors
teach.narration: Put two ohms over three ohms on the left, with l as the balance distance from the left end.

teach.title: Clear the fractions
teach.narration: Cross-multiply to get two hundred minus two l equals three l, then add two l to both sides to get five l.

teach.title: Solve for l
teach.narration: Divide two hundred by five to find the balance point is forty centimetres from the left side. Choose B.

steps.title: Use parallel voltage rule
steps.narration: In parallel, every branch gets the full twelve volts of the battery.

steps.title: Apply Ohm's law
steps.narration: Divide the twelve volts across the resistor by its twelve ohm resistance.

steps.title: Find branch current
steps.narration: Twelve divided by twelve equals one point zero amperes. Choose D.

teach.title: Focus on the 12 Ω branch
teach.narration: Pick out the twelve volt supply and the twelve ohm resistor. The two ohm and four ohm resistors are extra information we do not need because parallel branches do not change each other's voltage.

teach.title: Recall parallel voltage
teach.narration: Resistors in parallel are connected across the same two terminals of the battery, so each branch receives the full twelve volts.

teach.title: Apply Ohm's law
teach.narration: Use Ohm's law for that single branch: current equals potential difference divided by resistance.

teach.title: Calculate the current
teach.narration: Twelve divided by twelve gives one point zero amperes through the twelve ohm resistor. Choose D.

steps.title: Choose parallel connection
steps.narration: To lower resistance below two hundred ohms, connect another resistor in parallel.

steps.title: Use parallel formula
steps.narration: Subtract one over two hundred from one over one hundred and twenty using common denominator six hundred.

steps.title: Invert to find R
steps.narration: Two over six hundred simplifies to one over three hundred, so connect a three hundred ohm resistor in parallel. Choose A.

teach.title: Choose series or parallel
teach.narration: Adding a resistor in series raises resistance, while adding one in parallel opens another current path and lowers resistance. So we must connect R in parallel.

teach.title: State parallel formula
teach.narration: For two parallel resistors, the reciprocal of total resistance equals the sum of their reciprocals.

teach.title: Rearrange for R
teach.narration: Put in one hundred and twenty ohms and two hundred ohms, then subtract one over two hundred from both sides.

teach.title: Combine the fractions
teach.narration: Use six hundred as the common denominator: five minus three over six hundred simplifies to one over three hundred.

teach.title: Invert for resistance
teach.narration: Flipping one over three hundred gives three hundred ohms, connected in parallel. Choose A.

steps.title: Find parallel resistance
steps.narration: From the diagram, combine the three ohm and six ohm parallel resistors to get two ohms.

steps.title: Apply Ohm's law
steps.narration: With negligible internal resistance, multiply the four point zero ampere total current by two ohms.

steps.title: Find the e.m.f.
steps.narration: Four point zero times two gives eight volts. Choose D.

teach.title: Read the circuit diagram
teach.narration: From the diagram, cell E supplies a total current of four point zero amperes shown at the top into three ohm and six ohm resistors wired in parallel.

teach.title: Combine parallel resistors
teach.narration: For two resistors in parallel, use product over sum. Three times six over three plus six gives eighteen over nine, or two ohms.

teach.title: Use the circuit equation
teach.narration: Because internal resistance is negligible, no voltage is lost inside the cell, so the full e.m.f. equals total current times external resistance.

teach.title: Calculate the e.m.f.
teach.narration: Multiply four point zero amperes by two ohms to get an e.m.f. of eight volts. Choose D.

steps.title: Rearrange power formula
steps.narration: Use P equals V squared over R and multiply by R to isolate V squared.

steps.title: Substitute P and R
steps.narration: Multiply forty watts by ninety ohms to get three thousand six hundred.

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.narration: The square root of three thousand six hundred is sixty volts. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the instrument's normal power rating of forty watts and its resistance of ninety ohms.

teach.title: Choose the power formula
teach.narration: Choose the power equation written in terms of voltage and resistance because current is not given.

teach.title: Rearrange and substitute
teach.narration: Multiply both sides by resistance to make V squared the subject, then substitute forty watts and ninety ohms.

teach.title: Multiply the values
teach.narration: Forty times ninety equals three thousand six hundred.

teach.title: Take the square root
teach.narration: Take the square root of three thousand six hundred to undo the square, giving sixty volts. Choose A.

steps.title: Find input power
steps.narration: Multiply one point five amperes by two hundred and fifty volts to get three hundred and seventy-five watts.

steps.title: Apply 80% efficiency
steps.narration: At eighty percent efficiency, the useful power output is eighty percent of three hundred and seventy-five watts.

steps.title: Calculate power output
steps.narration: Zero point eight zero times three hundred and seventy-five equals three hundred point zero watts. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the motor's current, supply potential difference, and efficiency of eighty percent.

teach.title: Find electrical input power
teach.narration: Calculate the electrical power drawn from the supply by multiplying current and voltage, giving three hundred and seventy-five watts.

teach.title: Apply efficiency
teach.narration: Only eighty percent of the electrical input becomes useful mechanical output because the rest is lost as heat and friction.

teach.title: Compute power output
teach.narration: Four fifths of three hundred and seventy-five gives three hundred point zero watts. Choose A.

steps.title: Find max safe current
steps.narration: Each two ohm resistor has an eighteen watt limit, which gives a maximum safe current of three amperes.

steps.title: Find power in each resistor
steps.narration: From the diagram, three amperes goes through the series resistor and splits into one point five amperes through each parallel resistor.

steps.title: Add all three powers
steps.narration: Add eighteen, four point five, and four point five watts to get twenty-seven watts. Choose A.

teach.display: Two 2 Ω parallel + one 2 Ω series
teach.title: Read the circuit diagram
teach.narration: From the diagram, two two ohm resistors sit in parallel and are joined in series with a third two ohm resistor. Each resistor can handle at most eighteen watts.

teach.title: Find safe current limit
teach.narration: Use P equals I squared R to find the maximum current a single two ohm resistor can carry. Eighteen over two is nine, whose square root is three amperes.

teach.title: Check the series resistor
teach.narration: All the circuit current flows through the single series resistor, so it sets the limit at three amperes and dissipates its full eighteen watts.

teach.title: Split parallel current
teach.narration: At the equal parallel pair, three amperes divides evenly into one point five amperes per branch, so each parallel resistor dissipates four point five watts.

teach.title: Sum the total power
teach.narration: Add the power in all three resistors together to get a maximum total power of twenty-seven watts. Choose A.

steps.title: Rearrange power formula
steps.narration: Electrical power equals current times voltage, so divide power by voltage.

steps.title: Substitute the ratings
steps.narration: Put two thousand watts over two hundred and fifty volts.

steps.title: Find maximum current
steps.narration: Two thousand divided by two hundred and fifty gives eight amperes. Choose B.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the power rating of two thousand watts and the voltage rating of two hundred and fifty volts.

teach.title: Rearrange P = IV
teach.narration: Since power is current multiplied by voltage, divide power by voltage to find the maximum current the device draws.

teach.title: Substitute and simplify
teach.narration: Put two thousand watts on top and two hundred and fifty volts underneath, then cancel one zero from each.

teach.title: Divide for current
teach.narration: Two hundred divided by twenty-five equals eight amperes. Choose B.

steps.display: Magnetic N = 10° east of True N
steps.title: Place magnetic north
steps.narration: A declination of ten degrees east puts magnetic north ten degrees east of true north.

steps.title: Add the compass angle
steps.narration: The compass points forty degrees further east from magnetic north, giving fifty degrees east of true north.

steps.title: Write true bearing
steps.narration: The true geographic bearing is North fifty degrees East. Choose A.

teach.title: List the given angles
teach.narration: Write down the magnetic declination of ten degrees east and the compass bearing of North forty degrees East.

teach.display: Magnetic N is 10°E of True N
teach.title: Locate magnetic north
teach.narration: Declination is the angle between true north and magnetic north. Ten degrees east means the compass needle's north points ten degrees clockwise from true north.

teach.title: Add both eastward turns
teach.narration: The compass reads forty degrees east starting from magnetic north, so add ten degrees and forty degrees to measure the total angle from true north.

teach.title: State the true bearing
teach.narration: Measured from true geographic north, the bearing is North fifty degrees East. Choose A.

steps.title: Find total resistance
steps.narration: Divide one hundred volts by zero point zero five amperes to get two thousand ohms total.

steps.title: Subtract coil resistance
steps.narration: Subtract the galvanometer's ten ohm resistance to get one thousand nine hundred and ninety ohms.

steps.title: State the connection
steps.narration: Connect this multiplier resistor in series so it limits current at one hundred volts. Choose C.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the galvanometer resistance of ten ohms, its maximum safe current of zero point zero five amperes, and the target reading of one hundred volts.

teach.title: Choose series connection
teach.narration: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, add a high resistance in series so extra voltage drops across R and keeps current within zero point zero five amperes.

teach.tag: use Ohm's law for total R
teach.title: Use Ohm's law for total R
teach.narration: By Ohm's law, the combined series resistance equals full-scale voltage divided by maximum permissible current.

teach.title: Divide by 0.05
teach.narration: One hundred divided by zero point zero five equals ten thousand divided by five, which is two thousand ohms.

teach.title: Subtract internal resistance
teach.narration: Subtract the ten ohms of the galvanometer coil itself, leaving one thousand nine hundred and ninety ohms connected in series. Choose C.

steps.title: Find net reactance
steps.narration: Subtract the ten ohm capacitive reactance from the sixteen ohm inductive reactance to get six ohms.

steps.title: Calculate impedance
steps.narration: Combine the eight ohm resistance and six ohm net reactance by Pythagoras to get ten ohms.

steps.title: Find the current
steps.narration: Divide the twelve volt e.m.f. by the ten ohm impedance to get one point two amperes. Choose C.

teach.title: List the circuit values
teach.narration: Write down the e.m.f., the resistance, and both reactances in the series alternating current circuit.

teach.title: Find net reactance
teach.narration: Inductive and capacitive reactances oppose each other, so subtract ten ohms from sixteen ohms to get a net reactance of six ohms.

teach.title: State impedance formula
teach.narration: Because resistance and net reactance are ninety degrees out of phase, combine them using Pythagoras' theorem to find impedance.

teach.title: Compute the impedance
teach.narration: Eight squared plus six squared equals sixty-four plus thirty-six, or one hundred, whose square root is ten ohms.

teach.title: Find circuit current
teach.narration: Divide the twelve volt e.m.f. by the ten ohm impedance to get one point two amperes. Choose C.

steps.title: Find primary input power
steps.narration: Divide the fifty watt output power by zero point eight zero efficiency to get sixty-two point five watts input.

steps.title: Divide by primary voltage
steps.narration: Divide sixty-two point five watts by the two hundred volt mains voltage.

steps.title: Round primary current
steps.narration: Sixty-two point five over two hundred gives zero point three one two five, or zero point three one amperes. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the output power, the eighty percent efficiency, and the two hundred volt mains voltage on the primary side.

teach.title: Link efficiency to input
teach.narration: Because the transformer is only eighty percent efficient, the primary coil draws more power than the fifty watts delivered out.

teach.title: Calculate input power
teach.narration: Fifty divided by zero point eight zero equals five hundred divided by eight, which is sixty-two point five watts.

teach.title: Use primary power formula
teach.narration: Primary power equals primary current times primary voltage, so divide sixty-two point five watts by two hundred volts.

teach.title: Divide and round
teach.narration: Sixty-two point five divided by two hundred is zero point three one two five amperes, which rounds to zero point three one amperes. Choose A.

steps.title: State Faraday's first law
steps.narration: The mass deposited equals the electrochemical equivalent multiplied by the electric charge.

steps.title: Substitute z and Q
steps.narration: Multiply one point three times ten to the minus seven by two point zero times ten to the four.

steps.title: Simplify the answer
steps.narration: One point three times two is two point six, and minus seven plus four gives ten to the minus three kilograms. Choose D.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the electrochemical equivalent in kilograms per coulomb and the charge in coulombs, both already in SI units.

teach.title: State Faraday's formula
teach.narration: By Faraday's first law of electrolysis, mass deposited is proportional to total charge passed, with z as the proportionality constant.

teach.title: Substitute the values
teach.narration: Multiply the given electrochemical equivalent by the charge in coulombs.

teach.title: Multiply and add exponents
teach.narration: Multiply one point three by two point zero to get two point six, and add exponents minus seven and four to get minus three kilograms. Choose D.

steps.title: Find first charge
steps.narration: Multiply zero point five amperes by three hours to get one point five ampere-hours.

steps.title: Find second charge
steps.narration: Multiply one point five amperes by one hour to get one point five ampere-hours as well.

steps.title: Compare the charges
steps.narration: Because the same charge passes through the same metal, the mass deposited stays two grams. Choose C.

teach.title: Note the first case
teach.narration: Record the first current and time that deposit two grams. Since both times are in hours, we can compare current times time directly without converting to seconds.

teach.title: State Faraday's first law
teach.narration: Faraday's first law states that mass deposited of the same metal depends only on total charge Q equals I t.

teach.title: Compare both charges
teach.narration: Zero point five times three is one point five, and one point five times one is also one point five.

teach.title: Read deposited mass
teach.narration: The current tripled while the time fell to a third, so the total charge is identical and two grams is deposited again. Choose C.

steps.title: Use uncertainty principle
steps.narration: Use Heisenberg's relation delta x times delta p equals h and divide by delta x.

steps.title: Substitute h and Δx
steps.narration: Divide Planck's constant six point six times ten to the minus thirty-four by five times ten to the minus ten.

steps.title: Find momentum uncertainty
steps.narration: Six point six over five is one point three two, and subtracting minus ten from minus thirty-four gives minus twenty-four. Choose C.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the position uncertainty in metres and Planck's constant in joule seconds.

teach.title: State uncertainty relation
teach.narration: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle links position and momentum uncertainties through Planck's constant. Divide h by delta x to find the momentum uncertainty.

teach.title: Substitute the values
teach.narration: Put six point six times ten to the minus thirty-four on top and five times ten to the minus ten below.

teach.title: Divide and simplify powers
teach.narration: Six point six divided by five equals one point three two, and minus thirty-four minus minus ten equals minus twenty-four newton seconds. Choose C.

steps.title: Convert energy to joules
steps.narration: Multiply three point three electronvolts by one point six times ten to the minus nineteen to convert to joules.

steps.title: Use Planck's equation
steps.narration: Divide the energy in joules by Planck's constant.

steps.title: Find the frequency
steps.narration: Five point two eight over six point six is zero point eight, giving eight point zero times ten to the fourteen hertz. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the photon energy in electronvolts, the electronic charge, and Planck's constant six point six times ten to the minus thirty-four joule seconds.

teach.title: Convert eV to joules
teach.narration: Multiply electronvolts by the electron charge to get joules because Planck's constant uses SI units of joule seconds.

teach.title: Rearrange Planck's formula
teach.narration: Photon energy equals Planck's constant times frequency, so divide energy by h to isolate frequency.

teach.title: Substitute and divide
teach.narration: Five point two eight divided by six point six is zero point eight, and subtracting minus thirty-four from minus nineteen gives ten to the fifteen.

teach.title: Write in standard form
teach.narration: Rewrite zero point eight times ten to the fifteen as eight point zero times ten to the fourteen hertz. Choose A.

steps.title: Find photon energy
steps.narration: Multiply Planck's constant by the light frequency to find each photon's energy.

steps.title: Write in standard form
steps.narration: Six point six times six point seven is forty-four point two two, or four point four two two times ten to the minus nineteen joules.

steps.title: Subtract work function
steps.narration: Subtract the three times ten to the minus nineteen joule work function to get one point four two times ten to the minus nineteen joules. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the work function of caesium, the frequency of light, and Planck's constant.

teach.title: Compute photon energy
teach.narration: Find the energy delivered by one photon by multiplying six point six times ten to the minus thirty-four by six point seven times ten to the fourteen.

teach.title: Match the power of ten
teach.narration: Express the photon energy using ten to the minus nineteen so it matches the work function's power of ten before subtracting.

teach.title: State Einstein's equation
teach.narration: By Einstein's photoelectric equation, the work function frees the electron and the remaining photon energy becomes maximum kinetic energy.

teach.title: Subtract work function
teach.narration: Subtract three from four point four two two to get one point four two times ten to the minus nineteen joules. Choose A.

steps.title: Use energy level formula
steps.narration: The energy of level n equals the ground state energy divided by n squared.

steps.title: Substitute n = 3
steps.narration: For the third level, divide minus twenty-four point eight electronvolts by three squared, which is nine.

steps.title: Divide and match option
steps.narration: Minus twenty-four point eight over nine is minus two point seven six electronvolts, matching minus two point seven five electronvolts. Choose C.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Note the ground state energy at n equals one is minus twenty-four point eight electronvolts, and we need the third level where n equals three.

teach.title: State Bohr level formula
teach.narration: In an atom's energy levels, energy scales inversely with the square of the level number n.

teach.title: Substitute n = 3
teach.narration: Put minus twenty-four point eight on top and three squared, equal to nine, underneath.

teach.title: Divide and match option
teach.narration: Dividing minus twenty-four point eight by nine gives minus two point seven five five recurring electronvolts, which matches the keyed option minus two point seven five electronvolts. Choose C.

steps.title: Convert mass to kilograms
steps.narration: Change one point zero grams to one point zero times ten to the minus three kilograms.

steps.title: Find the mass defect
steps.narration: Zero point zero one percent of the mass gives one point zero times ten to the minus seven kilograms converted to energy.

steps.title: Apply E = mc squared
steps.narration: Multiply ten to the minus seven by three point zero times ten to the eight squared to get nine point zero times ten to the nine joules. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the one point zero gram sample, the zero point zero one percent mass decrease, and the speed of light.

teach.title: Change grams to kilograms
teach.narration: Divide one point zero grams by one thousand to convert to kilograms because energy in joules requires SI mass units.

teach.title: Calculate mass lost
teach.narration: Zero point zero one percent is ten to the minus four, so multiply ten to the minus four by ten to the minus three to get ten to the minus seven kilograms.

teach.title: Use Einstein's formula
teach.narration: Substitute the lost mass and speed of light into E equals delta m c squared. Squaring three point zero times ten to the eight gives nine point zero times ten to the sixteen.

teach.title: Simplify powers of ten
teach.narration: Add the exponents minus seven and sixteen to get nine. The fission energy is nine point zero times ten to the nine joules, option A.

steps.title: Count the half-lives
steps.narration: Divide eighty days by the twenty-day half-life to get four half-lives.

steps.title: Apply half-life decay
steps.narration: Each half-life halves the sample, so raise one half to the fourth power.

steps.title: Find remaining fraction
steps.narration: Two to the power of four is sixteen, so one sixteenth remains. Choose A.

teach.title: List what is given
teach.narration: Write down the half-life of twenty days and the total decay time of eighty days.

teach.title: Find number of half-lives
teach.narration: Divide total time by the half-life to see how many halving periods occur, which gives four half-lives.

teach.title: Halve four times
teach.narration: Each half-life leaves half of the remaining radioactive nuclei, so multiply by one half four times.

teach.title: Evaluate the power
teach.narration: Raise one half to the fourth power to get one sixteenth of the original nuclei remaining. Choose A.

steps.title: Find new mass number
steps.narration: Two alpha particles subtract eight from mass number two hundred and thirty-five, leaving two hundred and twenty-seven.

steps.title: Find new atomic number
steps.narration: Two alphas subtract four and three betas add three to atomic number ninety-two, giving ninety-one.

steps.title: Read both numbers
steps.narration: The daughter nucleus has mass number two hundred and twenty-seven and atomic number ninety-one. Choose A.

teach.title: Identify the emissions
teach.narration: An alpha particle carries mass four and charge two, a beta particle carries mass zero and charge minus one, and the gamma ray carries zero mass and zero charge so it does not change either number.

teach.title: Balance the mass number
teach.narration: Total mass number is conserved across the decay. Only the two alpha particles lower the mass number, each by four.

teach.title: Find daughter mass number
teach.narration: Subtract eight from two hundred and thirty-five to get a daughter mass number of two hundred and twenty-seven.

teach.title: Balance the atomic number
teach.narration: Total charge is conserved. Two alpha decays remove four protons, while three beta-minus decays increase the atomic number by three.

teach.title: Read both numbers
teach.narration: Ninety-two minus four plus three equals ninety-one. So the mass and atomic numbers are two hundred and twenty-seven and ninety-one, option A.
